title: There’s a Fatty Liver Epidemic. AI Could Help Get Ahead of It
gist: Fatty liver disease now affects roughly 30 percent of adults worldwide and over a billion people, yet three-quarters of cirrhosis patients are only diagnosed once the condition is life-threatening. Researchers argue AI run passively over existing electronic health records, routine blood panels, and incidental chest x-rays is the only workflow-compatible way to catch reversible disease early, with commercial products like Evido's LiverPRO (partnered with Roche) already outperforming the incumbent Fib-4 score.

themes.theme: Market size and the detection gap

insights.claim: Fatty liver disease now affects approximately 30 percent of adults worldwide, with liver fat exceeding 5 to 10 percent of organ weight in more than a billion people.
insights.speaker: David Cox
insights.so_what: A 30 percent adult prevalence defines an unusually large screening and therapeutics TAM for anyone selling diagnostics, GLP-1s, or liver-targeted drugs.
insights.locator: While the presence of fat in a normal, healthy liver

insights.claim: Three-quarters of people with cirrhosis or advanced liver scarring are only diagnosed once their condition has become life-threatening, because fatty liver disease typically develops without noticeable symptoms.
insights.speaker: David Cox
insights.so_what: The bottleneck is detection timing, not treatment availability, so value accrues to screening and triage tools rather than to new late-stage therapies.
insights.locator: Even in cases of cirrhosis or advanced scarring

insights.claim: Fatty liver disease has been linked to increased risk of cardiovascular disease and various cancers in addition to liver failure, making it an upstream driver of multiple high-cost disease categories.
insights.speaker: David Cox
insights.so_what: Cross-indication linkage strengthens the health-economic case payers need to fund population-level liver screening.
insights.locator: If left to linger, progressive fat accumulation

themes.theme: Reversibility makes early detection economically decisive

insights.claim: In early stages fatty liver damage is highly reversible through lifestyle changes including reduced alcohol intake, weight loss, exercise, and even drinking more coffee, which have been shown to reverse scarring and inflammation.
insights.speaker: David Cox
insights.so_what: Because the disease is reversible, a cheap detection tool captures most of the clinical value, which favors software margins over drug economics in early-stage patients.
insights.locator: If fatty liver disease can be identified early

insights.claim: For patients with moderate to advanced liver scarring, the GLP-1 medication semaglutide and the drug resmetirom have been shown to be highly effective therapeutics.
insights.speaker: David Cox
insights.so_what: Effective drugs already exist for the diagnosed population, so every incremental early diagnosis converts directly into pharma revenue, aligning drugmaker incentives with funding AI screening.
insights.locator: Even for people with moderate to advanced liver scarring

insights.claim: Hepatology has traditionally optimized for late-stage care and extending survival rather than early detection and prevention, despite the liver's capacity to regenerate and reverse fibrosis.
insights.speaker: David Cox
entities: CUNY Graduate School of Public Health and Health Policy
insights.so_what: A stated misallocation inside a specialty is the kind of gap that new entrants exploit; watch for screening-first startups displacing referral-driven incumbents.
insights.quote: The liver is a very versatile and interesting organ because it can regenerate, fibrosis can be reversed, and you can be completely healthy again,
insights.locator: The liver is a very versatile and interesting organ

insights.claim: Danish research found that informing people they have liver fibrosis makes them more likely to commit to dietary and exercise regimes, meaning diagnosis itself functions as a behavioral intervention.
insights.speaker: David Cox
insights.so_what: Diagnosis-as-treatment improves the ROI math on screening even before any drug is prescribed.
insights.locator: He points to research carried out in Denmark

insights.claim: Identifying and treating patients earlier would save health systems vast sums because liver transplants are extraordinarily expensive, particularly in the US.
insights.speaker: David Cox
insights.so_what: Transplant-cost avoidance is the reimbursement argument that gets a screening algorithm paid for by US payers.
insights.quote: Liver transplants are extraordinarily expensive in any country, but especially the US.
insights.locator: For health care systems grappling with a rising burden

themes.theme: Why AI, not more tests: the workflow constraint

insights.claim: Any new liver-screening step must run in the background or reduce to a single button press, because physicians facing growing workload and administrative burden will not sustainably absorb added testing.
insights.speaker: David Cox
insights.so_what: Clinician time, not accuracy, is the binding constraint for health AI adoption; products requiring new physician actions should be discounted heavily.
insights.quote: You have to have something that can run in the background or it’s easy to just hit a button and do it,
insights.locator: You have to have something that can run in the background

insights.claim: Simple noninvasive liver-health assessments already exist but are rarely used even in obviously high-risk groups such as people with obesity and type 2 diabetes.
insights.speaker: David Cox
insights.so_what: The failure is deployment, not technology, which favors vendors that automate existing scores over those developing novel biomarkers.
insights.locator: One of the frustrations for Lazarus and others

insights.claim: AI can retrospectively mine massive numbers of hospital visits and lab reports across electronic health records to prioritize who is most at risk, without requiring new patient encounters.
insights.speaker: David Cox
insights.so_what: Retrospective EHR mining is a zero-marginal-cost patient-finding channel, valuable to both health systems and pharma launching liver drugs.
insights.quote: AI can retrospectively go through massive numbers of hospital visits and lab reports,
insights.locator: AI can retrospectively go through massive numbers

insights.claim: Combining the Fib-4 index with the second-line enhanced liver fibrosis blood test has been shown to improve diagnosis of advanced fibrosis four-fold in patients with worrying liver fat levels.
insights.speaker: David Cox
insights.so_what: A quantified four-fold uplift from a two-test cascade sets the accuracy bar that AI alternatives must clear to justify replacing the standard pathway.
insights.locator: Using both of these tests in patients

themes.theme: Competing AI approaches and commercial traction

insights.claim: Danish health tech startup Evido's LiverPRO algorithm assesses liver fibrosis risk from age plus nine routine blood biomarkers and outperformed Fib-4 in predicting serious liver problems across more than 470,000 middle-aged people, and is being commercialized with Roche.
insights.speaker: David Cox
insights.so_what: A validated 470,000-patient outperformance plus a big-pharma distribution partner is the clearest commercial signal in the space and a template for diagnostics-pharma tie-ups.
insights.locator: As a result, the Danish health tech startup Evido

insights.claim: An AI model called ALADDIN, built on routine blood tests, outperformed Fib-4 and other risk scores at identifying which patients would benefit most from resmetirom, potentially replacing invasive liver biopsy for treatment selection.
insights.speaker: David Cox
insights.so_what: Biopsy-free patient selection removes the main friction on resmetirom uptake, a direct volume lever for that drug's manufacturer.
insights.locator: Other AI-based tests could also help doctors

insights.claim: An Osaka Metropolitan University model identified fatty liver disease from routine chest x-rays with 82 percent accuracy, exploiting the fact that scans aimed at the lungs and heart also capture parts of the liver.
insights.speaker: David Cox
insights.so_what: Opportunistic screening on already-acquired imaging is free at the point of care and could be layered onto every radiology AI installation as a paid add-on.
insights.locator: AI could also do this using x-ray images

insights.claim: Fib-4 is quick and low-cost but is less accurate in adolescents and seniors and raises concerns about false positives and unnecessary referrals unless combined with additional testing.
insights.speaker: David Cox
insights.so_what: The incumbent score's known weaknesses in specific age bands define the exact wedge for AI challengers like LiverPRO.
insights.locator: While Fib-4 is a quick and low-cost tool

insights.claim: AI liver tools will be adopted as a smarter first pass that fixes primary-care bottlenecks and reduces unnecessary hepatology referrals rather than replacing biopsies or imaging.
insights.speaker: David Cox
insights.so_what: Positions these products as triage software sold on referral-cost savings, not as substitutes for high-reimbursement diagnostic procedures.
insights.quote: But they could fix the bottlenecks in primary care where most fibrosis goes undetected.
insights.locator: These tools won’t completely replace biopsies

insights.claim: AI in liver care has so far been largely confined to research rather than clinical deployment, though proponents expect that to change soon.
insights.speaker: David Cox
insights.so_what: Sets the timing expectation: the category is pre-commercial, so near-term revenue estimates for liver AI should be treated skeptically.
